strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored niche: instance-level, physically interactable 3D tabletop scene generation for embodied AI, distinct from large-scale room generation methods.

The pipeline is thoughtfully decomposed into interpretable stages (instance extraction with generative completion, canonical 3D model generation, DRO for rotation, TSA for translation/scale), each targeting a specific known failure mode of prior single-image reconstruction approaches (occlusion, pose ambiguity, scale ambiguity).

The DRO tri-modal loss (silhouette + edge + DINOv2 appearance) is a reasonable and well-justified differentiable formulation for rotation recovery, and the RMA-Score for anchor selection in TSA is a sensible heuristic for resolving scale ambiguity via a top-view proxy.

Extensive empirical validation: quantitative comparison against three baselines (ACDC, Gen3DSR, MIDI) with perceptual, GPT-based, and collision metrics; a large-scale user study (128 participants); ablations isolating DRO and TSA; extensions to real-world images, scene editing, and stylized inputs; and a robotic manipulation demonstration in Isaac Sim.

Strong and consistent margins over baselines across nearly all reported metrics, particularly on collision rate (near-zero vs 8-17%/67-98%), suggesting the pose/scale alignment approach meaningfully improves physical plausibility.

Good transparency in supplementary material: prompts, stage-wise intermediate outputs, efficiency breakdown, and an honest discussion of a bias in the camera-sweep evaluation protocol (Sec 8.1) that could favor baselines, which is a commendable self-critical addition rather than a hidden flaw.
weaknesses: The method is a heavy orchestration of existing off-the-shelf components (ChatGPT, GroundedSAM-v2, Seedream, Hunyuan3D-3.0, DINOv2, Pytorch3D differentiable rendering) with two moderately novel algorithmic pieces (DRO loss, RMA-Score); the core technical novelty is somewhat incremental relative to the engineering complexity, and the paper does not clearly disentangle how much of the gain over baselines comes from the alignment stages versus simply using superior underlying image-to-3D and MLLM foundation models compared to the baselines' backbones.

Heavy reliance on proprietary/commercial black-box models (ChatGPT, Seedream, Hunyuan3D-3.0) raises reproducibility concerns; results may not be reproducible with open alternatives, and the "training-free" framing understates the dependence on very capable, closed foundation models that arguably do most of the heavy lifting (scene description, completion, size priors, stacking order).

Test set (78 samples) is relatively small and self-constructed without release details fully specified; no discussion of failure cases or limitations of the RMA-Score/anchor selection (e.g., what happens if all instances have moderate aspect-ratio error, or if MLLM commonsense size estimates are wrong for unusual objects) beyond a brief future-work paragraph.

Efficiency is a real concern: ~32 minutes per scene for 9 instances (with DRO alone taking ~90s per instance) is very slow for "large-scale generation" claims made in the introduction/abstract; no discussion of how this scales to denser scenes or larger-scale deployment for robot policy training data synthesis, which is the paper's core motivating use case.

The rotation is restricted to a single degree of freedom around the vertical axis (ri ∈ R), which may be insufficient for tabletop objects placed in non-canonical orientations (e.g., tilted books, leaning objects), though this simplification is not explicitly justified or its limitations discussed.

GPT-4o is used both to help generate scene descriptions/priors during pipeline execution and as an evaluator (GPT Evaluation metric), which raises a potential circularity/self-preference concern that is not addressed or controlled for.

The comparison to MesaTask (a directly relevant recent text-driven tabletop baseline) is only qualitative (2 examples) rather than quantitative, since the paper argues text-based generation lacks consistent references for fair comparison — but this leaves the core text-to-scene claim less rigorously validated than the image-to-scene claim.

Physical plausibility metrics (collision rate) are the primary quantitative measure of "physical plausibility," but no evaluation of stability under actual physics simulation (e.g., whether objects remain in place after gravity settles, or success rates of the downstream manipulation tasks beyond qualitative video demonstration) is quantitatively reported in the main paper.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: most 3D scene generation work targets room-scale layouts, while tabletop scenes with dense, small, functionally-related objects pose distinct challenges; the paper articulates this gap clearly with concrete criteria (instance quality, functional layout, collision-free spatial relations).

The pose/scale alignment sub-problem is tackled with a reasonably well-motivated technical design: the tri-modal (silhouette+edge+DINOv2 appearance) differentiable rotation loss and the RMA-Score anchor-selection mechanism for scale/translation are sensible, non-trivial engineering solutions to single-view ambiguity.

Extensive empirical validation: quantitative comparison against three baselines across perceptual, GPT-4o-judged, and collision metrics, a large-scale user study (128 participants), component-wise ablations (DRO/TSA), qualitative text-driven comparison to MesaTask, real-world image tests, scene-editing demos, and a robotic manipulation demonstration in Isaac Sim.

Commendable transparency about a potential metric bias: the authors explicitly discuss how the camera-sweep best-view LPIPS protocol can mask physically implausible baseline outputs, arguing their real advantage is likely understated rather than hiding the issue.

Substantial supplementary material (stage-wise intermediate outputs, prompts, JSON outputs, efficiency breakdown) supports reproducibility of the pipeline logic even though some components are closed-source.
weaknesses: Heavy dependence on closed-source, proprietary components (ChatGPT/GPT-4o for essentially all reasoning steps, Seedream for image synthesis/completion, Hunyuan3D-3.0 for image-to-3D) undermines reproducibility and scientific rigor; the "training-free" framing somewhat obscures that most of the system's intelligence is delegated to black-box commercial APIs whose behavior may change over time and cannot be independently verified or re-run without cost.

Using GPT-4o both as an evaluator (VF/IA/PP/OR metrics) and as a core component of the generation pipeline (MLLM reasoning throughout) raises a circularity/self-preference concern that is not discussed or mitigated.

No quantitative comparison to MesaTask, the most directly relevant prior work (also targeting task-driven tabletop scene generation); only a small qualitative comparison (two examples) is provided, which is insufficient to substantiate claims of superiority over the closest baseline.

The chosen quantitative baselines (ACDC, Gen3DSR, MIDI) are general single-image 3D scene reconstruction methods not designed for high-density tabletop layouts, making the comparison somewhat favorable to a method specifically engineered for this setting; this should be acknowledged more directly as a fairness caveat.

Reported runtime (~32 minutes per 9-object scene) is slow, which conflicts with the stated motivation of enabling "automated, large-scale generation" of tabletop scenes for embodied-AI policy training/data synthesis at scale.

The technical contribution is largely an integration of many existing off-the-shelf modules (GroundedSAM, DINOv2, Pytorch3D, Hunyuan3D, Isaac Sim) glued together with prompt engineering; the genuinely novel algorithmic content is confined to the DRO/TSA alignment stage, and the framework offers no analysis of error propagation or failure modes across its many sequential stages.

The rotation model is restricted to a single yaw angle about the vertical axis, which, while reasonable for tabletop objects resting flat, is a simplification not extensively justified or stress-tested for objects with non-trivial resting orientations.

Test set size (78 samples) is modest for the breadth of claims made (state-of-the-art across styles, shapes, and functional categories), and no failure-case analysis or discussion of when the pipeline breaks down (e.g., very small or thin objects, severe occlusion, ambiguous stacking) is provided in the main paper.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and practical gap: existing 3D scene generation methods (retrieval-based, LLM room-scale, single-image reconstruction) are shown to be poorly suited for producing simulation-ready, collision-free tabletop scenes for manipulation data synthesis.

The decoupled Pose and Scale Alignment design (DRO for rotation via a tri-modal silhouette/edge/appearance loss, TSA for translation/scale via top-view synthesis, stacking priors, and an RMA-Score anchor selection) is a sensible, tabletop-specific technical contribution that directly targets the failure modes of prior compositional methods (depth-based pose estimation errors, lack of physical priors).

Comprehensive empirical validation: quantitative comparisons against multiple image-driven (ACDC, Gen3DSR, MIDI) and text-driven (MesaTask, Holodeck-table) baselines, plus additional comparisons with SceneGen and FlashSculptor in the supplementary, consistently show large margins, especially in collision-rate metrics (Col_O near 0.4% vs 8-21% for baselines).

A large-scale user study (128 participants) supports the automated GPT-4o evaluation and shows strong human preference (83% overall preference) for the proposed method, strengthening the claim of perceptual superiority.

The zero-shot real-to-sim-to-real policy transfer experiment (training π0.5 purely on synthetic trajectories and deploying on a physical AgileX PiPER arm without real-world fine-tuning) is a valuable and rare form of validation that demonstrates practical downstream utility beyond visual/metric benchmarks.
Thorough ablations (w/o DRO, w/o TSA, w/o both) with both quantitative and qualitative evidence isolate the contribution of each alignment component.

Very detailed supplementary material (prompts, stage-wise intermediate outputs, camera-sweep protocol, user-study interface, additional stability metrics SS/DSS) supports reproducibility and transparency, and the authors candidly discuss a potential fairness bias in the best-view evaluation protocol favoring baselines.

The system supports useful downstream capabilities (in-scene editing: add/remove/replace/rearrange) enabling low-cost scene diversity expansion, which is relevant for large-scale data engine use cases.
weaknesses: The pipeline is deeply reliant on a chain of proprietary, closed-source foundation models (ChatGPT/GPT-4o for reasoning and evaluation, Seedream for image synthesis, GroundedSAM-v2, Hunyuan3D-3.0) at nearly every stage; while described as 'training-free', this reliance raises reproducibility, cost, latency, and long-term-availability concerns that are not discussed.

Using GPT-4o both to guide/complete the generation pipeline (commonsense sizes, stacking relations, category recognition) and as the primary automatic evaluator (VF/IA/PP/OR scores) creates a degree of evaluator-generator entanglement that could bias the reported GPT-based metrics in the method's favor; the paper does not discuss this potential circularity.

The zero-shot real-to-sim-to-real validation, while compelling, covers only three simple pick-and-place/stacking tasks on a single real scene and a single robot platform (AgileX PiPER) with 50 trials each; broader task and scene diversity for the sim-to-real claim would strengthen generalization evidence.

All objects are treated as rigid bodies with convex-decomposition collision geometry; articulated or deformable objects (drawers, boxes with lids, soft goods) common on real tabletops are not addressed, limiting the scope of 'physical plausibility' claims.

Physical stability metrics (Support Stability, Dynamic Settling Stability) that could better substantiate 'physical plausibility' claims are only reported for the supplementary comparison against SceneGen/FlashSculptor, not for the main baselines (ACDC, Gen3DSR, MIDI, MesaTask, Holodeck-table) in the primary tables, leaving a gap in the main quantitative story.

Test set size (78 scenes for image-driven, 30 text-scene pairs for text-driven comparison) is modest, and while diversity axes are described, statistical robustness (e.g., variance, confidence intervals) of the reported metrics is not provided.

The novelty is primarily in system integration and the DRO/TSA alignment strategy rather than a fundamentally new generative model; the differentiable rendering rotation optimization and top-view-based layout inference build heavily on established techniques (differentiable rendering, DINOv2 features, LLM-based commonsense reasoning), which somewhat limits the algorithmic contribution despite strong systems-level execution.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: generating physically plausible, instance-interactive tabletop scenes for robotic manipulation data synthesis, filling a gap between room-scale generative scene methods and asset-library-limited tabletop methods (e.g., MesaTask).

The technical pipeline is clearly decomposed and each component is well justified: generative instance extraction with mask completion for occlusion handling, a Differentiable Rotation Optimizer with a sensible tri-modal loss (silhouette, edge, DINOv2 appearance), and a Top-View Spatial Alignment module with a principled RMA-Score for anchor selection that combines area and aspect-ratio consistency.

Extensive and multi-faceted evaluation: quantitative comparisons against both image-driven (ACDC, Gen3DSR, MIDI) and text-driven (MesaTask, Holodeck-table) baselines, a large-scale user study with 128 participants, GPT-4o-based multi-dimensional scoring, and thorough ablations isolating DRO and TSA contributions.

The zero-shot real-to-sim-to-real policy transfer experiment (training π0.5 purely on synthetic trajectories and deploying directly on a physical AgileX PiPER arm) is a strong and convincing piece of evidence for the practical utility of the generated data, going beyond purely visual/simulated metrics.

Physical plausibility is evaluated with meaningful, non-trivial metrics (collision rates, and in the supplementary, Support Stability and Dynamic Settling Stability), and the paper is refreshingly self-critical about potential biases in its own best-view evaluation protocol, providing a mean-view analysis to address this.

Supplementary material is unusually thorough (stage-wise intermediate outputs, prompts, additional baselines SceneGen/FlashSculptor, user-study UI details), aiding reproducibility and transparency despite reliance on proprietary components.
weaknesses: The core system is largely an orchestration of existing large pretrained models (ChatGPT/GPT-4o, Seedream, Hunyuan3D-3.0, GroundedSAM-v2), with the primary original technical content residing in the pose/scale alignment (DRO+TSA) stage; the paper should be judged as an applied/systems contribution rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic/generative technique, which somewhat limits its intrinsic novelty even though the engineering integration is solid.

Heavy dependence on closed, proprietary APIs (GPT-4o, Seedream) raises reproducibility concerns, since these models may change over time, incur ongoing cost, and are not fully controllable/inspectable by other researchers attempting to replicate results.

GPT-4o is used both implicitly in the generation pipeline (semantic reasoning, size priors, stacking relations) and as an evaluator (VF/IA/PP scoring), which introduces a degree of potential circularity/self-consistency bias in the automatic evaluation, only partially mitigated by the independent human user study.

The test set (78 scenes) and the real-to-sim-to-real validation (only 3 tasks, 50 trials each) are relatively modest in scale for claims of a general-purpose 'data engine'; more diverse manipulation tasks, object categories, and larger-scale policy training/evaluation would strengthen the impact claims.

The method is restricted to rigid objects on a single flat tabletop and does not address articulated/deformable objects or more complex support structures (shelves, drawers), which the authors acknowledge as future work but somewhat narrows current applicability.

No detailed analysis of failure cases or computational cost/latency per scene is provided, which would be useful for assessing the practicality of scaling this pipeline to generate very large synthetic datasets.
